Abstract. A smooth manifold tells us what it means to move and differentiate, but it does not determine a dynamics. A Poisson structure adds an antisymmetric bracket on smooth functions that turns each function into a vector field and each Hamiltonian into an evolution law. This post develops that idea from canonical Hamiltonian mechanics, passes from the algebraic bracket to the intrinsic Poisson bivector, explains the Jacobi identity and its coordinate form, and shows how a possibly degenerate Poisson manifold decomposes into symplectic leaves. The main examples are canonical phase space, two-dimensional Poisson structures, and the Lie–Poisson structure on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
A smooth manifold provides a stage on which calculus can be performed. At a point $p \in M$, it supplies a tangent space $T_pM$, a cotangent space $T_p^*M$, and smooth functions whose differentials belong to those cotangent spaces. But the manifold alone does not tell us how a point should move, which quantities should be conserved, or how two observables should interact.
A Poisson structure supplies precisely this additional layer. Its central object is a bracket
$$ \lbrace \cdot, \cdot \rbrace : C^\infty(M) \times C^\infty(M) \longrightarrow C^\infty(M), $$which converts smooth functions into infinitesimal motions. Once a Hamiltonian function $H$ is chosen, the bracket determines a vector field $X_H$ and therefore a differential equation. Unlike a symplectic form, however, a Poisson structure is allowed to be degenerate. Its effective phase-space dimension may vary from point to point.
The guiding principle of this article is therefore:
$$ \boxed{\text{A Poisson manifold is a smooth manifold foliated by symplectic phase spaces.}} $$This sentence is only a preview. To understand it properly, we must explain the bracket, its Jacobi identity, the bivector hidden behind it, and the symplectic leaves on which the dynamics actually takes place.
Throughout, manifolds are finite-dimensional smooth real manifolds, Hausdorff and second countable, without boundary unless stated otherwise. Functions, vector fields, and tensor fields are smooth, and all functions are real-valued. The sign convention for Hamiltonian vector fields is fixed in Section 1 and used consistently thereafter.
1. From phase space to the Poisson bracket Consider the canonical phase space $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with coordinates
$$ (q^1, \ldots, q^n, p_1, \ldots, p_n), $$where $q^i$ denotes a position coordinate and $p_i$ its conjugate momentum. Given a Hamiltonian $H \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{2n})$, Hamilton’s equations are
$$ \dot q^i = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}, \qquad \dot p_i = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n. $$These equations define the Hamiltonian vector field
$$ X_H = \sum_{i = 1}^n \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q^i} - \frac{\partial H}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i}\right). $$If $f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^{2n})$ is an observable and $\gamma(t)$ is a trajectory satisfying $\dot\gamma(t) = X_H\vert_{\gamma(t)}$, then the chain rule gives
$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}f(\gamma(t)) = X_H(f)(\gamma(t)). $$The right-hand side can be written using the canonical Poisson bracket
$$ \lbrace f, g \rbrace = \sum_{i = 1}^n \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q^i} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial q^i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}\right). \tag{1.1} $$With this sign convention,
$$ X_H(f) = \lbrace H, f \rbrace, $$so Hamilton’s equations become
$$ \dot q^i = \lbrace H, q^i \rbrace, \quad \dot p_i = \lbrace H, p_i \rbrace. $$Some texts use the negative bracket and consequently write
$$ \dot{f} = \lbrace f, H \rbrace. $$Both conventions describe the same geometry, but one must not switch between them in the middle of a calculation.
The bracket immediately expresses conservation laws. An observable $f$ is constant along the Hamiltonian flow precisely when
$$ \lbrace H, f \rbrace = 0. $$In particular, the Hamiltonian is conserved because the bracket is antisymmetric:
$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}H(\gamma(t)) = \lbrace H, H \rbrace = 0. $$Historically, the bracket arose in Poisson’s study of mechanics, while the identity now bearing Jacobi’s name explains why the bracket of two conserved quantities is again conserved; a concise modern account is given by Bursztyn (2025). The modern differential-geometric theory was shaped in particular by Lichnerowicz (1977) and Weinstein (1983). The decisive conceptual step is to retain the structural properties of (1.1) without insisting on canonical coordinates or even on an even-dimensional ambient manifold.
2. The definition of a Poisson manifold Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, and let $C^\infty(M)$ denote the real vector space of smooth functions $M \to \mathbb{R}$.
Definition (Poisson bracket). A Poisson bracket on $M$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-bilinear map $\lbrace \cdot, \cdot \rbrace : C^\infty(M) \times C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ such that, for all $f, g, h \in C^\infty(M)$, the following three properties hold:
Skew-symmetry: $\lbrace f, g \rbrace = -\lbrace g, f \rbrace$. Jacobi identity: $\lbrace f, \lbrace g, h \rbrace \rbrace + \lbrace g, \lbrace h, f \rbrace \rbrace + \lbrace h, \lbrace f, g \rbrace \rbrace = 0$. Leibniz rule: $\lbrace f, gh \rbrace = \lbrace f, g \rbrace h + g \lbrace f, h \rbrace$. Definition (Poisson manifold). A Poisson manifold is a pair $(M, \lbrace \cdot, \cdot \rbrace)$ consisting of a smooth manifold $M$ and a Poisson bracket on $C^\infty(M)$.
This is the standard smooth definition used, for example, by Bursztyn (2025, Section 2.1) and Crainic et al. (2021).
The three axioms have different jobs.
Skew-symmetry and the Jacobi identity say that $C^\infty(M)$ is a Lie algebra under $\lbrace \cdot, \cdot \rbrace$. The Leibniz rule says that the bracket is compatible with the ordinary pointwise product of functions. Thus $C^\infty(M)$ simultaneously carries a commutative multiplication and a Lie bracket, tied together by a first-order differentiation rule. This combined object is called a Poisson algebra.
Because of skew-symmetry, the Leibniz rule also holds in the first argument. Indeed,
$$ \lbrace fg, h \rbrace = -\lbrace h, fg \rbrace = -\lbrace h, f \rbrace g - f \lbrace h, g \rbrace = f \lbrace g, h \rbrace + g \lbrace f, h \rbrace. $$Therefore the bracket is a derivation in each argument separately.
2.1 Why the Leibniz rule matters Fix $f \in C^\infty(M)$. The map
$$ D_f : C^\infty(M) \longrightarrow C^\infty(M), \qquad D_f(g) = \lbrace f, g \rbrace, $$is a derivation. A fundamental fact from differential geometry says that derivations of $C^\infty(M)$ are exactly smooth vector fields. Consequently, there is a unique vector field $X_f \in \mathfrak{X}(M)$ satisfying
$$ X_f(g) = \lbrace f, g \rbrace \qquad\text{for every }g \in C^\infty(M). \tag{2.1} $$This is the Hamiltonian vector field generated by $f$.
The Leibniz rule is therefore what converts an algebraic operation on functions into a geometric direction of motion. Without it, $g \mapsto \lbrace f, g \rbrace$ need not be a vector field and the bracket would not define a local dynamics on $M$.
2.2 Why the Jacobi identity matters The Jacobi identity is not a decorative algebraic condition. Applying (2.1) to a test function $h$ gives
$$ \begin{aligned} [X_f, X_g](h) &= X_f(X_g(h)) - X_g(X_f(h))\\ &= \lbrace f, \lbrace g, h \rbrace \rbrace - \lbrace g, \lbrace f, h \rbrace \rbrace \\ &= \lbrace \lbrace f, g \rbrace, h \rbrace \\ &= X_{\lbrace f, g \rbrace}(h). \end{aligned} $$Since this holds for every $h$, we obtain
$$ \boxed{[X_f, X_g] = X_{\lbrace f, g \rbrace}.} \tag{2.2} $$Thus the assignment $f \mapsto X_f$ preserves Lie brackets. Equation (2.2) has several consequences:
Hamiltonian vector fields are closed under commutators. Hamiltonian flows preserve the Poisson structure. If $f$ and $g$ are conserved by $H$, then $\lbrace f, g \rbrace$ is also conserved, because the Jacobi identity gives $\lbrace H, \lbrace f, g \rbrace \rbrace = 0$. If skew-symmetry and the Leibniz rule hold but the Jacobi identity fails, one has an almost-Poisson bracket. Such a bracket still produces vector fields, but their commutators need not correspond to the bracket of their Hamiltonians. This failure is precisely the obstruction measured by the Jacobi identity.
3. From a bracket to a bivector field The definition above is algebraic: it speaks about pairs of smooth functions. Differential geometry offers an equivalent tensorial description.
At a point $p \in M$, the value $\lbrace f, g \rbrace(p)$ depends only on the differentials $\mathrm{d}f\vert_p$ and $\mathrm{d}g\vert_p$. One way to see this is to fix one argument and use the fact that a derivation at $p$ is determined by a tangent vector at $p$. Bilinearity and the derivation property in both arguments then imply the existence of a unique alternating bilinear form on $T_p^*M$ whose value on $\mathrm{d}f\vert_p$ and $\mathrm{d}g\vert_p$ is $\lbrace f, g \rbrace(p)$.
As $p$ varies, these alternating bilinear forms fit together smoothly.
Definition (Poisson bivector). The bivector field associated with a Poisson bracket is the section $\pi \in \Gamma(\wedge^2 TM)$ determined by
$$ \boxed{\lbrace f, g \rbrace = \pi(\mathrm{d}f, \mathrm{d}g).} \tag{3.1} $$A bivector is the contravariant counterpart of a differential $2$-form. A $2$-form eats two tangent vectors, whereas a bivector eats two covectors:
$$ \omega_p : T_pM \times T_pM \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad \pi_p : T_p^*M \times T_p^*M \to \mathbb{R}. $$The bivector defines a bundle map
$$ \pi^\sharp : T^*M \longrightarrow TM $$by the rule
$$ \beta\bigl(\pi^\sharp(\alpha)\bigr) = \pi(\alpha, \beta), \qquad \alpha, \beta \in T_p^*M. \tag{3.2} $$Comparing (3.1), (3.2), and (2.1), we find
$$ \boxed{X_f = \pi^\sharp(\mathrm{d}f).} \tag{3.3} $$This formula displays the logical chain of Poisson dynamics:
$$ f\ \longmapsto\ \mathrm{d}f\ \longmapsto\ \pi^\sharp(\mathrm{d}f) = X_f\ \longmapsto\ \text{flow of }X_f. $$The smooth function supplies a covector field, and the Poisson tensor converts those covectors into tangent directions.
3.1 The local coordinate formula Let $(x^1, \ldots, x^m)$ be local coordinates on an open set $U \subseteq M$. Every bivector field on $U$ can be written as
$$ \pi = \frac12\sum_{i, j = 1}^m\pi^{ij}(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}, \qquad \pi^{ij} = -\pi^{ji}. \tag{3.4} $$The factor $1/2$ compensates for summing over both $(i, j)$ and $(j, i)$. Substituting (3.4) into (3.1) gives
$$ \lbrace f, g \rbrace = \sum_{i, j = 1}^m\pi^{ij}(x)\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x^j}. \tag{3.5} $$In particular,
$$ \pi^{ij} = \lbrace x^i, x^j \rbrace. $$The Hamiltonian vector field of $f$ is therefore
$$ X_f = \sum_{i, j = 1}^m\pi^{ij}(x)\frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}. \tag{3.6} $$Equations (3.4)–(3.6) are coordinate expressions of intrinsic objects. The coefficient functions $\pi^{ij}$ change under a change of coordinates, but the bivector $\pi$, the bracket, and the vector field $X_f$ do not depend on the chosen chart.
4. The Jacobi identity in coordinates Not every bivector field defines a Poisson bracket. Any bivector defines an antisymmetric biderivation through (3.1), but its bracket may fail the Jacobi identity. We now translate the missing condition into a differential equation for the coefficients $\pi^{ij}$.
Because the Jacobiator
$$ \operatorname{Jac}(f, g, h) = \lbrace f, \lbrace g, h \rbrace \rbrace + \lbrace g, \lbrace h, f \rbrace \rbrace + \lbrace h, \lbrace f, g \rbrace \rbrace $$is a derivation in each argument, it is represented by a trivector field. It is therefore enough to evaluate it on coordinate functions. Since $\lbrace x^j, x^k \rbrace = \pi^{jk}$, we obtain
$$ \lbrace x^i, \lbrace x^j, x^k \rbrace \rbrace = \lbrace x^i, \pi^{jk} \rbrace = \sum_{\ell = 1}^m\pi^{i\ell}\frac{\partial\pi^{jk}}{\partial x^\ell}. $$Adding the cyclic permutations gives the coordinate Jacobi condition:
$$ \boxed{ \sum_{\ell = 1}^m \left( \pi^{i\ell}\frac{\partial\pi^{jk}}{\partial x^\ell} + \pi^{j\ell}\frac{\partial\pi^{ki}}{\partial x^\ell} + \pi^{k\ell}\frac{\partial\pi^{ij}}{\partial x^\ell} \right) = 0 } \tag{4.1} $$for every $i, j, k \in \lbrace 1, \ldots, m \rbrace$.
This nonlinear first-order system is the coordinate test for a Poisson bivector. It immediately yields two useful facts.
First, every constant bivector is Poisson because all derivatives in (4.1) vanish. Canonical phase space is an example.
Second, every bivector on a two-dimensional manifold is Poisson. The Jacobiator is a trivector, but $\wedge^3 T_pM = \lbrace 0 \rbrace$ when $\dim M = 2$. Thus, in local coordinates $(x, y)$, every bivector
$$ \pi = \varphi(x, y)\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \qquad \varphi \in C^\infty(M), \tag{4.2} $$defines a Poisson structure.
The corresponding statement is false in dimension three. For example, on $\mathbb{R}^3$ consider the bivector determined by
$$ \lbrace x, y \rbrace = x, \qquad \lbrace y, z \rbrace = y, \qquad \lbrace z, x \rbrace = z. $$Its Jacobiator on the coordinate functions is
$$ \lbrace x, \lbrace y, z \rbrace \rbrace + \lbrace y, \lbrace z, x \rbrace \rbrace + \lbrace z, \lbrace x, y \rbrace \rbrace = x + y + z, $$which is not identically zero. This is an almost-Poisson structure, not a Poisson structure.
4.1 The intrinsic Jacobi condition There is also a coordinate-free test. The Schouten–Nijenhuis bracket extends the Lie bracket of vector fields to multivector fields. For a bivector $\pi$, the expression $[\pi, \pi]_{\mathrm{SN}}$ is a trivector, and its coefficients are exactly the left-hand side of (4.1), up to the conventional normalization. Hence
$$ \boxed{\pi\text{ is Poisson}\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad [\pi, \pi]_{\mathrm{SN}} = 0.} \tag{4.3} $$Equation (4.3) is the intrinsic tensor form of the Jacobi identity. It is especially valuable in deformation theory and Poisson cohomology, but the coordinate condition (4.1) is usually the more concrete entry point. Both descriptions are developed systematically by Crainic et al. (2021) and Bursztyn (2025, Sections 2.2–2.3).
5. Fundamental examples Examples reveal what the definition allows and why Poisson geometry is broader than symplectic geometry.
5.1 The zero Poisson structure Every smooth manifold admits the trivial bracket
$$ \lbrace f, g \rbrace = 0\qquad\text{for all }f, g \in C^\infty(M). $$Equivalently, $\pi = 0$. Every Hamiltonian vector field vanishes, so every Hamiltonian trajectory is stationary. This example is degenerate in the strongest possible sense, but it is a legitimate Poisson manifold.
This observation is conceptually important: being a Poisson manifold imposes no restriction on the dimension or topology of the underlying smooth manifold. The nontrivial information lies in the chosen tensor $\pi$.
5.2 Symplectic manifolds A symplectic manifold is a pair $(M, \omega)$ in which $\omega \in \Omega^2(M)$ is closed and nondegenerate. Nondegeneracy means that
$$ \omega^\flat : TM \longrightarrow T^*M, \qquad \omega^\flat(X) = \iota_X\omega, $$is a vector-bundle isomorphism. Therefore each $f \in C^\infty(M)$ determines a unique vector field $X_f$ through
$$ \iota_{X_f}\omega = \mathrm{d}f. \tag{5.1} $$Define
$$ \lbrace f, g \rbrace = \mathrm{d}g(X_f) = \omega(X_g, X_f). \tag{5.2} $$The closedness condition $\mathrm{d}\omega = 0$ implies that this bracket satisfies the Jacobi identity. Equivalently, the inverse bundle map
$$ \pi^\sharp = (\omega^\flat)^{-1} : T^*M \longrightarrow TM $$defines a nondegenerate Poisson bivector. Conversely, every nondegenerate Poisson bivector arises from a unique symplectic form in this way. Thus
$$ \boxed{\text{symplectic structures}\quad \longleftrightarrow \quad\text{nondegenerate Poisson structures}.} \tag{5.3} $$On canonical phase space, the symplectic form is
$$ \omega_{\mathrm{can}} = \sum_{i = 1}^n\mathrm{d}q^i \wedge \mathrm{d}p_i, $$and its inverse Poisson bivector, in the convention of this article, is
$$ \pi_{\mathrm{can}} = \sum_{i = 1}^n\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial q^i}. $$Formula (3.1) then reproduces the canonical bracket (1.1).
5.3 Poisson structures on surfaces Let $M$ be a two-dimensional manifold. As observed after (4.2), every smooth bivector field on $M$ is Poisson. On $\mathbb{R}^2$, take
$$ \pi = \varphi(x, y)\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial y}. $$The bracket is
$$ \lbrace f, g \rbrace = \varphi(x, y) \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\right). \tag{5.4} $$Where $\varphi \neq 0$, the Poisson structure is nondegenerate and therefore symplectic. Where $\varphi = 0$, its rank drops to zero. A single Poisson structure can consequently contain open two-dimensional regions of genuine motion and lower-dimensional sets on which every Hamiltonian vector field vanishes.
For example, if $\varphi(x, y) = x$, then the half-planes $x > 0$ and $x < 0$ are two-dimensional symplectic regions, while every point on the line $x = 0$ is a zero-dimensional symplectic leaf. This is the simplest picture of a singular Poisson manifold.
5.4 A Lie–Poisson structure on $\mathbb{R}^3$ Let $\boldsymbol{\xi} = (x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Define
$$ \lbrace f, g \rbrace(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \bigl(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \times \nabla g(\boldsymbol{\xi})\bigr). \tag{5.5} $$Equivalently,
$$ \pi = z\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial y} + x\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + y\frac{\partial}{\partial z} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial x}. \tag{5.6} $$This is the linear Poisson structure on the dual of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. Its coefficients are not constant, but they satisfy the Jacobi condition because the cross product encodes the Lie bracket of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$.
Consider the function
$$ C(x, y, z) = \frac12(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). $$For every $g \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)$,
$$ \lbrace C, g \rbrace = \boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \bigl(\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \nabla g\bigr) = 0. $$Thus $X_C = 0$, even though $C$ is not constant on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Its level sets are spheres, and Hamiltonian dynamics generated by any $H$ remains on one of these spheres. The origin is exceptional: the bivector vanishes there.
For a rigid body with principal moments of inertia $I_1, I_2, I_3$, the Hamiltonian
$$ H(x, y, z) = \frac{x^2}{2I_1} + \frac{y^2}{2I_2} + \frac{z^2}{2I_3} $$produces Euler’s rigid-body equations under this bracket. The motion is confined simultaneously to a level set of $H$ and a sphere $C = \text{constant}$. This example, discussed by Bursztyn (2025, Example 2.6), illustrates why degenerate Poisson structures are natural in mechanics: constraints on motion are encoded directly by the degeneracy of $\pi$.
6. Rank and the characteristic distribution The bundle map $\pi^\sharp : T^*M \to TM$ need not be invertible. At each $p \in M$, define the rank of $\pi$ at $p$ by
$$ \operatorname{rank}\pi\vert_p = \operatorname{rank}\bigl(\pi_p^\sharp : T_p^*M \to T_pM\bigr). $$Because $\pi_p$ is skew-symmetric, this rank is always even. The image
$$ \mathcal{D}_p = \pi_p^\sharp(T_p^*M) \subseteq T_pM \tag{6.1} $$is the space of all instantaneous directions generated by Hamiltonian functions at $p$. Indeed,
$$ \mathcal{D}_p = \left\lbrace X_f\vert_p \,\middle\vert\, f \in C^\infty(M) \right\rbrace. $$The union
$$ \mathcal{D} = \pi^\sharp(T^*M) \subseteq TM $$is called the characteristic distribution of the Poisson structure.
If the rank of $\pi$ is constant, $\mathcal{D}$ is a vector subbundle of $TM$, and the Poisson manifold is called regular. If the rank varies, $\mathcal{D}$ is a singular distribution: its fibers still form vector subspaces, but their dimensions need not be locally constant.
The Jacobi identity enters once again. By (2.2), commutators of Hamiltonian vector fields are Hamiltonian, so the family of directions in $\mathcal{D}$ is closed under Lie brackets. In the regular case, the Frobenius theorem then implies that $\mathcal{D}$ is tangent to a foliation. In the singular case, integrability is more subtle, but it still holds for Poisson structures; this follows locally from Weinstein’s splitting theorem.
7. Symplectic leaves Definition (symplectic leaf). A symplectic leaf of a Poisson manifold $(M, \pi)$ is a maximal connected immersed submanifold $\iota : \mathcal{O}\hookrightarrow M$ satisfying
$$ T_p\mathcal{O} = \mathcal{D}_p = \pi_p^\sharp(T_p^*M) $$for every $p \in \mathcal{O}$.
This definition and the resulting symplectic foliation are developed in Bursztyn (2025, Section 4.1); their singular local structure is governed by Weinstein’s theorem below.
Every point of $M$ lies on exactly one symplectic leaf. Since $\mathcal{D}p$ has even dimension, every leaf is even-dimensional. The tangent bivector induced by $\pi$ on a leaf is nondegenerate, and its inverse defines a symplectic form $\omega{\mathcal{O}}$ on that leaf.
More concretely, if $f, g \in C^\infty(M)$ and $p \in \mathcal{O}$, the leafwise symplectic form is characterized by
$$ \omega_{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(X_g\vert_p, X_f\vert_p\bigr) = \lbrace f, g \rbrace(p). \tag{7.1} $$This is well defined even if several functions generate the same tangent vector: if $X_f\vert_p = 0$, then $\lbrace f, g \rbrace(p) = \mathrm{d}g\vert_p(X_f\vert_p) = 0$ for every $g$. The Jacobi identity implies that $\mathrm{d}\omega_{\mathcal{O}} = 0$, so $\omega_{\mathcal{O}}$ is genuinely symplectic. Conversely, a smooth symplectic foliation determines the Poisson tensor by inverting the symplectic form along each leaf; the smoothness requirement is essential.
The phrase “foliated by symplectic phase spaces” can now be understood literally:
a Hamiltonian vector field is tangent to every symplectic leaf; a Hamiltonian trajectory can never jump from one leaf to another; within each leaf, the dynamics is ordinary symplectic Hamiltonian dynamics; different leaves may have different dimensions when the Poisson rank is not constant. For the zero Poisson structure, every leaf is a point. For a symplectic manifold, the connected components of $M$ are the leaves. For the surface structure $\pi = x, \partial_x \wedge \partial_y$, the two open half-planes are two-dimensional leaves and each point of the line $x = 0$ is a zero-dimensional leaf. For the Lie–Poisson structure (5.6), the nonzero leaves are the spheres centered at the origin, while the origin itself is a point leaf.
One subtlety is worth emphasizing: leaves are generally immersed, not necessarily embedded. A leaf can wind densely through part of the ambient manifold. The word “foliation” must therefore be interpreted in the regular or singular geometric sense, not as a guarantee that the leaf space $M/\mathcal{O}$ is a well-behaved manifold.
8. Casimir functions Definition (Casimir). A function $C \in C^\infty(M)$ is a Casimir function if
$$ \lbrace C, f \rbrace = 0\qquad\text{for every }f \in C^\infty(M). \tag{8.1} $$Equivalently,
$$ X_C = 0\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \pi^\sharp(\mathrm{d}C) = 0. $$By skew-symmetry, (8.1) also gives $X_f(C) = \lbrace f, C \rbrace = 0$ for every Hamiltonian $f$. Hence a Casimir is constant along every Hamiltonian trajectory and, more strongly, constant on every connected symplectic leaf.
Casimirs and ordinary first integrals play different roles:
A first integral of a particular Hamiltonian $H$ satisfies $\lbrace H, f \rbrace = 0$ and depends on the chosen dynamics. A Casimir satisfies $\lbrace g, C \rbrace = 0$ for every $g$ and is determined by the Poisson structure itself. On a symplectic manifold, $\pi^\sharp$ is invertible, so $\pi^\sharp(\mathrm{d}C) = 0$ implies $\mathrm{d}C = 0$. Therefore Casimirs are locally constant, and they are constant when the manifold is connected. Nonconstant Casimirs are a signature of degeneracy.
In favorable regular regions, sufficiently many independent Casimirs locally describe the symplectic leaves as their common level sets. If $M$ has dimension $m$, $\pi$ has constant rank $2r$, and one can find $m - 2r$ Casimirs with linearly independent differentials, then connected components of their common level sets are the symplectic leaves.
This is not a global theorem without additional hypotheses. A Poisson manifold may have too few global Casimir functions to separate its leaves, and its leaf space may be singular or non-Hausdorff. It is therefore safer to regard Casimirs as useful detectors of leaves, not as a universal global coordinate system for the leaf space.
9. Poisson maps The natural maps in Poisson geometry are those that preserve brackets.
Definition (Poisson map). Let $(M_1, \lbrace \cdot, \cdot \rbrace_1)$ and $(M_2, \lbrace \cdot, \cdot \rbrace_2)$ be Poisson manifolds. A smooth map $\Phi : M_1 \to M_2$ is a Poisson map if
$$ \lbrace f, g \rbrace_2 \circ \Phi = \lbrace f \circ \Phi, g \circ \Phi \rbrace_1 \tag{9.1} $$for all $f, g \in C^\infty(M_2)$.
Equation (9.1) says that pulling functions back by $\Phi$ preserves the Poisson algebra. It also implies compatibility of Hamiltonian vector fields: the Hamiltonian vector field of $f \circ \Phi$ on $M_1$ is $\Phi$-related to the Hamiltonian vector field of $f$ on $M_2$.
In tensorial language, the same condition is
$$ \pi_2^\sharp\vert_{\Phi(p)} = \mathrm{d}_p\Phi \circ \pi_1^\sharp\vert_p \circ (\mathrm{d}_p\Phi)^*, \tag{9.2} $$where $(\mathrm{d}p\Phi)^* : T{\Phi(p)}^*M_2 \to T_p^*M_1$ is the cotangent pullback.
If $\Phi$ is a Poisson diffeomorphism, it maps symplectic leaves of $M_1$ to symplectic leaves of $M_2$ and restricts to a symplectomorphism on each leaf. Thus Poisson diffeomorphisms preserve both the singular decomposition into leaves and the symplectic geometry carried by those leaves.
For a diffeomorphism between symplectic manifolds, preserving the symplectic forms is equivalent to being a Poisson map. The two conditions are not equivalent for a general, noninvertible smooth map: a form-preserving map must be an immersion, whereas a Poisson map may instead be a submersion. Invertibility is what makes the covariant condition on forms and the contravariant condition on bivectors equivalent.
10. Weinstein’s local splitting theorem The central local structure theorem for Poisson manifolds was proved by Weinstein (1983). It explains why symplectic leaves are the correct local building blocks.
Theorem (Weinstein splitting theorem). Let $(M, \pi)$ be an $m$-dimensional Poisson manifold, and suppose that $\pi$ has rank $2r$ at $p \in M$. Then there are local coordinates $(q^1, \ldots, q^r, p_1, \ldots, p_r, y^1, \ldots, y^s)$ centered at $p$, where $s = m - 2r$, in which $\pi$ takes the following form:
$$ \pi = \sum_{i = 1}^r\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial q^i} + \frac12\sum_{a, b = 1}^s\varphi^{ab}(\mathbf y)\frac{\partial}{\partial y^a} \wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial y^b}, \qquad \varphi^{ab}(\mathbf 0) = 0. \tag{10.1} $$Here each coefficient $\varphi^{ab}$ depends only on the transverse coordinates $\mathbf y = (y^1, \ldots, y^s)$. The first term in (10.1) is a canonical symplectic Poisson structure. The second is a transverse Poisson structure that vanishes at the chosen point. Locally, therefore, a Poisson manifold splits into
$$ \text{a symplectic factor}\quad \times \quad\text{a transverse Poisson factor vanishing at the base point}. $$Several important facts follow.
The Poisson rank at a point is even. Through every point passes a symplectic leaf of dimension equal to that rank. If the rank is locally constant, the transverse term vanishes throughout a sufficiently small neighborhood, so the Poisson tensor has the canonical form $\sum_i\partial_{p_i} \wedge \partial_{q^i}$ there. If $\pi$ is nondegenerate, there is no transverse factor, and the theorem reduces to Darboux’s theorem for symplectic manifolds. The theorem does not say that every singular Poisson structure is locally linear, nor does it remove all transverse complexity. It isolates that complexity in the $\mathbf y$ variables. Understanding when the transverse structure can be simplified further is a deeper problem in Poisson geometry.
11. What a Poisson structure does—and does not—provide It is useful to separate the data supplied by a Poisson structure from geometric structures that must be chosen independently.

No canonical bracket Yes Yes, nondegenerate No canonical bracket Does every function generate a vector field? No canonical choice Yes, $X_f = \pi^\sharp(\mathrm{d}f)$ Yes, uniquely via $\omega$ A gradient exists via the metric, but it is not Hamiltonian May the effective dynamical dimension vary? Not specified Yes No Not determined by the metric Are distances and angles defined? No No No Yes Is a particular dynamics selected? No No; a Hamiltonian $H$ is still required No; a Hamiltonian $H$ is still required No; an evolution law is still required In particular, a Poisson structure is not a metric. It does not measure lengths, angles, or distances. It is also not itself a dynamical system: it provides the mechanism $H \mapsto X_H$, but one must still choose the Hamiltonian.
Nor is a Poisson structure merely an antisymmetric matrix in coordinates. A coordinate matrix represents a bivector field, and its entries must transform tensorially between charts. If the entries vary with position, they must also satisfy the nonlinear Jacobi condition (4.1).
12. Common misconceptions 12.1 “Every Poisson manifold is symplectic” False. A Poisson manifold is symplectic only when $\pi^\sharp : T^*M \to TM$ is invertible everywhere. The zero bracket and the Lie–Poisson structure on $\mathbb{R}^3$ are Poisson but not symplectic.
12.2 “A Poisson manifold must have even dimension” False. Its symplectic leaves have even dimensions, but the ambient manifold can have any dimension. The three-dimensional Lie–Poisson example is the standard counterexample.
12.3 “Skew-symmetry and the Leibniz rule are sufficient” False in dimensions three and higher. They define an almost-Poisson bracket. The Jacobi identity is an independent differential constraint, as the nonexample following (4.2) demonstrates.
12.4 “A Casimir has zero differential” Not necessarily. A Casimir satisfies $\pi^\sharp(\mathrm{d}C) = 0$. Its differential may be nonzero but lie in the kernel of $\pi^\sharp$. Only in the symplectic case does invertibility force $\mathrm{d}C = 0$.
12.5 “Symplectic leaves are always embedded level surfaces” False. Locally, regular leaves often look like common level sets of Casimirs, and many familiar examples are embedded. Globally, leaves may be immersed but not embedded, and there may not be enough global Casimirs to describe them.
12.6 “The Jacobi identity is only an algebraic convention” False. It ensures the closure relation $[X_f, X_g] = X_{\lbrace f, g \rbrace}$, the invariance of the Poisson tensor under Hamiltonian flows, and the integrability that ultimately leads to symplectic leaves.
13. Final perspective The definition of a Poisson manifold can be read in three mutually reinforcing ways.
The algebraic viewpoint begins with observables. The space $C^\infty(M)$ is both a commutative algebra and a Lie algebra, and the Leibniz rule connects these two structures.
The tensorial viewpoint packages the bracket into a bivector $\pi$. The Jacobi identity becomes the geometric differential equation $[\pi, \pi]_{\mathrm{SN}} = 0$, while $\pi^\sharp$ converts differentials into Hamiltonian vector fields.
The foliated viewpoint follows the image of $\pi^\sharp$. Its integral manifolds are symplectic leaves, and every Hamiltonian trajectory remains inside one leaf. Degeneracy is not a defect: it records which directions are dynamically accessible and which quantities, such as Casimirs, constrain all Hamiltonian motion.
These viewpoints fit into one chain:
$$ \boxed{ \text{Poisson bracket} \ \longleftrightarrow \ \text{Poisson bivector} \ \longrightarrow \ \text{Hamiltonian vector fields} \ \longrightarrow \ \text{symplectic leaves} } $$The essential message is that Poisson geometry extends Hamiltonian mechanics beyond a single nondegenerate phase space. It allows phase spaces with constraints, singularities, symmetries, and variable rank while retaining a coherent notion of Hamiltonian evolution. That is why Poisson manifolds appear naturally wherever geometry, dynamics, and algebra meet.

summary: Abstract. A smooth manifold tells us what it means to move and differentiate, but it does not determine a dynamics. A Poisson structure adds an antisymmetric bracket on smooth functions that turns each function into a vector field and each Hamiltonian into an evolution law. This post develops that idea from canonical Hamiltonian mechanics, passes from the algebraic bracket to the intrinsic Poisson bivector, explains the Jacobi identity and its coordinate form, and shows how a possibly degenerate Poisson manifold decomposes into symplectic leaves. The main examples are canonical phase space, two-dimensional Poisson structures, and the Lie–Poisson structure on $\mathbb{R}^3$.
title: Poisson Manifolds

content:
Abstract. A smooth manifold is a space that may be globally curved or topologically complicated while remaining locally indistinguishable from Euclidean space. This post introduces this concept from first principles. We begin with topology, charts, transition maps, and atlases; then define smooth functions and smooth maps without assuming that the manifold sits inside a larger Euclidean space. From there, we construct tangent and cotangent spaces, differentials, vector fields, integral curves, flows, and Lie brackets. The sphere serves as a recurring example, allowing each abstract definition to be compared with familiar geometry. The central theme is that coordinates make calculations possible, while compatibility under coordinate changes makes the resulting mathematics intrinsic.
Imagine a tiny observer living on the surface of a sphere. The observer can draw a local map, measure two coordinates, differentiate functions, and follow curves without ever leaving the surface. What the observer cannot do is describe the entire sphere by one regular Cartesian coordinate system. Any single map must either omit a point, overlap itself, or become singular somewhere.
This is exactly the problem that manifold theory solves. A manifold is allowed to require many local maps, provided that the maps agree smoothly wherever they overlap. Calculus is performed inside the maps, while the compatibility of the maps guarantees that the answers describe the underlying space rather than a particular choice of coordinates.
The guiding principle is therefore
$$\boxed{\text{A smooth }d\text{-dimensional manifold is locally modeled on }\mathbb{R}^d.}$$The word locally carries most of the meaning. A circle is locally a line but is not globally a line. A sphere is locally a plane but is not globally a plane. Manifold theory turns this local Euclidean behavior into a rigorous setting for calculus.
Convention. Unless stated otherwise, every manifold in this article is finite-dimensional, Hausdorff, second countable, smooth, and without boundary.
The terminology and conventions below follow the standard treatments of Lee (2012) and Tu (2011). The topological preliminaries are consistent with Lee (2011).
1. Why Euclidean calculus is not enough Classical multivariable calculus is formulated on open subsets
$$\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d.$$The openness of $\Omega$ matters. If $x \in \Omega$, then sufficiently small changes of every coordinate remain inside $\Omega$. This makes ordinary partial derivatives, directional derivatives, and differential equations available near $x$.
Many natural spaces do not have this global form. The unit sphere
$$S^2 = \left\lbrace (x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1 \right\rbrace$$is not an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$. It is nevertheless two-dimensional: near every point, two independent parameters describe all nearby points of the sphere.
This reveals two notions of dimension:
the ambient dimension, which is the dimension of a surrounding space in a particular realization; the intrinsic dimension, which is the number of coordinates needed locally on the space itself. For $S^2 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$, the ambient dimension is three, whereas the intrinsic dimension is two. Manifold theory is built around intrinsic dimension. In fact, a manifold need not be presented as a subset of any Euclidean space at all.
The basic strategy is simple:
cover the space by coordinate neighborhoods; identify each neighborhood with an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$; use ordinary calculus in each coordinate representation; require that overlapping representations be related by smooth changes of coordinates. The rest of the theory makes these four steps precise.
2. The topological foundation Differentiability presupposes continuity, and continuity presupposes a topology. We therefore begin one level below smooth geometry.
2.1 Topological spaces and continuous maps A topology on a set $M$ is a collection $\mathcal{T}$ of subsets of $M$, called open sets, satisfying:
$\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$ and $M \in \mathcal{T}$; an arbitrary union of members of $\mathcal{T}$ belongs to $\mathcal{T}$; a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal{T}$ belongs to $\mathcal{T}$. The pair $(M, \mathcal{T})$ is a topological space. Usually the topology is understood and we simply write $M$.
A map $F : M \to N$ between topological spaces is continuous if
$$F^{-1}(V)\text{ is open in }M\text{ whenever }V\text{ is open in }N.$$A homeomorphism is a bijection $F : M \to N$ such that both $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are continuous. Homeomorphic spaces have the same topology: they may look different as subsets of larger spaces, but their neighborhoods and continuous maps have the same structure.
2.2 Topological manifolds Definition (topological manifold). Let $d$ be a nonnegative integer. A topological space $M$ is a topological manifold of dimension $d$ if it is locally Euclidean of dimension $d$, Hausdorff, and second countable.
Let us unpack the three conditions.
Locally Euclidean of dimension $d$. For every $p \in M$, there are an open neighborhood $U \subseteq M$ of $p$ and a homeomorphism $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$, where $\varphi(U)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
Hausdorff. If $p, q \in M$ and $p \neq q$, there are disjoint open sets $U, V \subseteq M$ such that $p \in U$ and $q \in V$.
Second countable. There is a countable family of open sets $\mathcal{B} = \left\lbrace B_1, B_2, \ldots \right\rbrace$ such that every open subset of $M$ is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$.
The Hausdorff condition guarantees, among other things, uniqueness of limits. Second countability rules out spaces that are locally reasonable but globally too large for standard analysis. A Hausdorff, second-countable topological manifold is paracompact; after a smooth structure is chosen, this makes smooth partitions of unity available. These global consequences are developed carefully by Lee (2011) and Lee (2012, Chapter 2).
The dimension $d$ is intrinsic. By invariance of domain, nonempty open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ cannot be homeomorphic when $d \neq m$. Thus the local dimension cannot change from chart to chart; see Lee (2011).
At this stage, $M$ supports topology but not yet calculus. A homeomorphism need not be differentiable, so we must specify which local coordinate systems are smoothly compatible.
3. Charts: local coordinate systems Definition (coordinate chart). A coordinate chart on a topological $d$-manifold $M$ is a pair $(U, \varphi)$ in which $U \subseteq M$ is open and $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U)$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset $\varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$.
The set $U$ is the coordinate neighborhood, and $\varphi$ is the coordinate map. If
$$\varphi(p) = \bigl(x^1(p), \ldots, x^d(p)\bigr),$$then the component functions
$$x^i = \operatorname{pr}_i \circ \varphi : U \to \mathbb{R}$$are the coordinate functions. The ordered tuple $(x^1(p), \ldots, x^d(p))$ gives the coordinates of $p$ in this chart.
The inverse map
$$\varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to U$$can be regarded as a local parameterization of the manifold. The coordinate map assigns numbers to points; its inverse turns coordinate values back into points.
It is useful to keep four related notions separate:
$(U, \varphi)$ is the chart; $\varphi$ is the coordinate map; $x^1, \ldots, x^d$ are the coordinate functions; $x^1(p), \ldots, x^d(p)$ are the coordinate values of $p$. In informal writing, “choose coordinates $(x^1, \ldots, x^d)$” usually means “choose a chart whose component functions are $(x^1, \ldots, x^d)$.”
3.1 Why the chart image must be open The requirement that $\varphi(U)$ be open in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ensures that ordinary multivariable calculus applies at every coordinate point. For each $x \in \varphi(U)$, a sufficiently small Euclidean ball around $x$ remains in the coordinate domain.
If chart images were allowed to have arbitrary boundaries or corners, the local differential calculus would depend on the shape of those images. Manifolds with boundary are handled by changing the local model in a controlled way; we return to them in Section 11.
4. Overlapping charts and smooth structures A manifold generally requires more than one chart. The crucial question is then: when do two coordinate systems describe the same smooth geometry?
4.1 Why one chart may not suffice The Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$ has the global chart $(\mathbb{R}^d, \operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{R}^d})$. The circle
$$S^1 = \left\lbrace (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : x^2 + y^2 = 1 \right\rbrace$$has no global chart taking it onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Indeed, $S^1$ is compact, whereas every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is noncompact. Because compactness is preserved by homeomorphisms, such a chart cannot exist.
Locally, however, one coordinate is enough. On the upper semicircle
$$U_+ = \left\lbrace (x, y) \in S^1 : y > 0 \right\rbrace,$$the map
$$\varphi_+(x, y) = x$$is a chart with inverse
$$\varphi_+^{-1}(u) = \left(u, \sqrt{1 - u^2}\right), \qquad -1 < u < 1.$$Other charts cover the parts omitted by $U_+$. The circle is therefore locally, but not globally, an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
4.2 Transition maps Let $(U, \varphi)$ and $(V, \psi)$ be charts with $U \cap V \neq \varnothing$. A point $p \in U \cap V$ has two coordinate descriptions:
$$x = \varphi(p), \qquad y = \psi(p).$$The change from $x$-coordinates to $y$-coordinates is the transition map
$$\psi \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U \cap V) \to \psi(U \cap V).$$Both its domain and codomain are open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$, so ordinary Euclidean differentiability applies.
Definition (smooth compatibility). Two charts are smoothly compatible if their domains are disjoint or their transition map is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism.
Because the transition map is bijective, this means that both $\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}$ and its inverse $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ are infinitely differentiable.
In coordinates, smooth compatibility says that the functions
$$y^a = y^a(x^1, \ldots, x^d), \qquad a = 1, \ldots, d,$$and the inverse functions
$$x^i = x^i(y^1, \ldots, y^d), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, d,$$are smooth. The Jacobian matrices of these transformations are inverse at every point of the overlap.
4.3 Atlases and maximal atlases Definition (smooth atlas). A smooth atlas on $M$ is a collection $\mathcal{A} = \left\lbrace (U_\alpha, \varphi_\alpha) \right\rbrace_{\alpha \in I}$ of pairwise smoothly compatible charts whose domains cover $M$:
$$M = \bigcup_{\alpha \in I}U_\alpha.$$Two smooth atlases are equivalent if every chart in one is smoothly compatible with every chart in the other. Equivalent atlases define the same notion of smoothness.
Every smooth atlas is contained in a unique maximal smooth atlas: the collection of all charts smoothly compatible with the original atlas. “Maximal” does not mean that the individual chart domains are as large as possible. It means that no additional compatible chart has been left out.
Definition (smooth manifold). A smooth $d$-manifold is a topological $d$-manifold equipped with a maximal smooth atlas.
In practice, one almost never writes down the maximal atlas. A convenient atlas is specified, and the compatible maximal atlas is understood.
This construction is standard; Lee (2012, Chapter 1) also explains why specifying any smooth atlas determines a unique maximal atlas. The definition may be summarized as
$$\boxed{\text{smooth manifold} = \text{topological manifold} + \text{smoothly compatible local coordinates}.}$$The topology determines which neighborhoods and maps are continuous. The smooth structure determines which functions and coordinate changes are differentiable.
5. Fundamental examples and nonexamples Examples reveal what the definition permits—and what it rules out.
5.1 Euclidean spaces and open subsets The identity chart gives $\mathbb{R}^d$ its standard smooth structure:
$$\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{R}^d} : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d.$$Every open subset $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is likewise a smooth $d$-manifold with the restricted identity chart.
5.2 The sphere For $d \geq 1$, define
$$S^d = \left\lbrace x = (x^1, \ldots, x^{d + 1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d + 1} : \sum_{i = 1}^{d + 1} (x^i)^2 = 1 \right\rbrace.$$Let
$$N = (0, \ldots, 0, 1), \qquad S = (0, \ldots, 0, -1)$$be the north and south poles, and set $U_N = S^d \setminus \left\lbrace N \right\rbrace$ and $U_S = S^d \setminus \left\lbrace S \right\rbrace$. Stereographic projection defines charts
$$\varphi_N(x) = \frac{(x^1, \ldots, x^d)}{1 - x^{d + 1}}, \qquad \varphi_S(x) = \frac{(x^1, \ldots, x^d)}{1 + x^{d + 1}}.$$Both maps take values in $\mathbb{R}^d$. On the overlap, if $u = \varphi_N(x) \neq 0$, then
$$\bigl(\varphi_S \circ \varphi_N^{-1}\bigr)(u) = \frac{u}{\lVert u \rVert^2}.$$This transition map is smooth on $\mathbb{R}^d \setminus \left\lbrace 0 \right\rbrace$ and is its own inverse. Hence the two stereographic charts form a smooth atlas on $S^d$. Because each chart uses $d$ coordinates, $\dim S^d = d$.
5.3 Products and tori If $M$ and $N$ are smooth manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$, their product has a natural smooth structure of dimension $m + n$. Product charts are given by
$$(U \times V, \varphi \times \psi), \qquad (\varphi \times \psi)(p, q) = (\varphi(p), \psi(q)).$$In particular,
$$T^d = (S^1)^d$$is a smooth $d$-manifold. The two-dimensional torus $T^2 = S^1 \times S^1$ may be visualized as the familiar doughnut-shaped surface, but its product definition is intrinsic and does not depend on an embedding in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
5.4 Matrix groups Identify the vector space of real $n \times n$ matrices with $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$. Since the determinant is continuous,
$$GL(n, \mathbb{R}) = \left\lbrace A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} : \det A \neq 0 \right\rbrace$$is open in $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$. It is therefore a smooth manifold of dimension $n^2$.
5.5 A crossing is not a manifold Consider the union of the two coordinate axes,
$$X = \left\lbrace (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : xy = 0 \right\rbrace.$$Away from the origin, $X$ locally resembles an open interval. At the origin, removing the origin from a sufficiently small neighborhood produces four connected pieces. Removing one point from an open interval produces at most two. Therefore no neighborhood of the origin is homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$, and $X$ is not a one-dimensional manifold.
The failure is topological, not merely a lack of smoothness. No choice of coordinates can repair the branching at the origin.
6. Smooth functions and smooth maps Charts allow Euclidean calculus to be transported to an abstract manifold.
6.1 Smooth real-valued functions Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. A function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth at $p \in M$ if there is a chart $(U, \varphi)$ containing $p$ such that
$$f \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi(U) \to \mathbb{R}$$is smooth in the ordinary Euclidean sense. The function is smooth on $M$ if it is smooth at every point.
This condition is independent of the chosen chart. If $(V, \psi)$ is another chart at $p$, then on the overlap
$$f \circ \psi^{-1} = (f \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}).$$The first map on the right is smooth by assumption, and the second is a smooth transition map. Their composition is smooth. This small calculation is the basic mechanism behind coordinate independence throughout differential geometry.
The vector space—and, under pointwise multiplication, commutative algebra—of smooth real-valued functions is denoted by $C^\infty(M)$.
6.2 Smooth maps between manifolds Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, and let $F : M \to N$ be a map. Choose a chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ and a chart $(V, \psi)$ on $N$. Wherever $F(U)$ meets $V$, the coordinate representation is
$$\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1} : \varphi\bigl(U \cap F^{-1}(V)\bigr) \to \psi(V).$$ Definition (smooth map). The map $F$ is smooth if it is continuous and every such local coordinate representation is a smooth map between open subsets of Euclidean spaces.
The continuity assumption is redundant if smooth coordinate representations are required around every point, because those local representations are continuous. Including it here makes the logical order transparent. The chart-based definitions in this section agree with the intrinsic definitions in Lee (2012, Chapter 2) and Tu (2011, Chapters 2 and 3).
A bijective smooth map whose inverse is smooth is a diffeomorphism. Diffeomorphic manifolds are equivalent as smooth manifolds. A homeomorphism preserves topology; a diffeomorphism preserves topology together with the smooth structure.
6.3 Smooth curves A smooth curve in $M$ is a smooth map
$$\gamma : I \to M,$$where $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is an open interval. In a chart, the curve becomes
$$(\varphi \circ \gamma)(t) = \bigl(x^1(t), \ldots, x^d(t)\bigr).$$The coordinate functions $x^i(t)$ can be differentiated by ordinary calculus. Their derivatives will lead us to the intrinsic notion of a tangent vector.
7. Tangent vectors: intrinsic velocities The tangent line to a plane curve or the tangent plane to a surface is usually drawn inside an ambient Euclidean space. An abstract manifold may have no preferred ambient space, so its tangent vectors must be defined intrinsically.
There are two complementary descriptions:
a tangent vector is the velocity of a curve through a point; a tangent vector is a derivation that differentiates smooth functions at that point. The curve description supplies the geometry. The derivation description captures exactly what the velocity does to observable functions.
7.1 Tangent vectors as equivalence classes of curves Fix $p \in M$. Let $\mathcal{C}_p$ be the collection of smooth curves $\gamma : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to M$ satisfying $\gamma(0) = p$, where $\varepsilon > 0$ may depend on the curve.
Choose a chart $(U, \varphi)$ around $p$. Two curves $\gamma_1, \gamma_2 \in \mathcal{C}_p$ are declared equivalent if
$$\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_{t = 0}(\varphi \circ \gamma_1)(t) = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_{t = 0}(\varphi \circ \gamma_2)(t).$$This relation does not depend on the chart. If $(V, \psi)$ is another chart around $p$, then
$$\psi \circ \gamma = (\psi \circ \varphi^{-1}) \circ (\varphi \circ \gamma),$$and the Euclidean chain rule gives
$$\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_{0}(\psi \circ \gamma)(t) = D(\psi \circ \varphi^{-1})_{\varphi(p)}\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_{0}(\varphi \circ \gamma)(t).$$Equal velocities in $\varphi$-coordinates therefore remain equal in $\psi$-coordinates.
Definition (tangent vector). A tangent vector at $p$ is an equivalence class $[\gamma]$ of curves through $p$ under the preceding relation.
The tangent vector represented by $\gamma$ is denoted by $\dot{\gamma}(0)$ or $\gamma’(0)$. The collection of all tangent vectors at $p$ is the tangent space $T_pM$.
7.2 The vector-space structure and coordinate basis The chart $(U, \varphi)$ identifies $T_pM$ with $\mathbb{R}^d$ through
$$[\gamma] \longmapsto \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_0(\varphi \circ \gamma)(t).$$We use this identification to add tangent vectors and multiply them by scalars. Because changes of coordinates act through invertible linear Jacobian maps, the resulting vector-space structure is independent of the selected chart. Consequently,
$$\dim T_pM = d.$$For sufficiently small $t$, define
$$\gamma_i(t) = \varphi^{-1}\bigl(\varphi(p) + t e_i\bigr),$$where $e_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The tangent vector $\dot{\gamma}_i(0)$ is denoted by
$$\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right\rvert_p.$$The vectors
$$\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^1}\right\rvert_p, \ldots, \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^d}\right\rvert_p$$form the coordinate basis of $T_pM$. Every $v \in T_pM$ has a unique representation
$$\boxed{v = \sum_{i = 1}^d v^i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right\rvert_p.}$$If $v = \dot{\gamma}(0)$, then
$$v^i = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_0 x^i(\gamma(t)).$$The numbers $v^i$ are components of the vector relative to the coordinate basis; they are not the vector itself.
7.3 Tangent vectors as derivations Let $C_p^\infty(M)$ denote the algebra of germs of smooth functions at $p$. Informally, two functions determine the same germ if they agree on some neighborhood of $p$. A derivation at $p$ is a linear map
$$v : C_p^\infty(M) \to \mathbb{R}$$satisfying the Leibniz rule
$$v[fg] = f(p)v[g] + g(p)v[f].$$A curve velocity defines a derivation by
$$\dot{\gamma}(0)[f] = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_0 f(\gamma(t)).$$This depends only on the germ of $f$ near $p$. In local coordinates, if $v = \sum_i v^i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right\rvert_p$, then
$$\boxed{v[f] = \sum_{i = 1}^d v^i \frac{\partial(f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x^i}\bigl(\varphi(p)\bigr).}$$Conversely, every derivation at $p$ has this form. To see the decisive step, write $a = \varphi(p)$ and $h = f \circ \varphi^{-1}$. On a sufficiently small coordinate neighborhood, the smooth Hadamard formula gives
$$h(u) - h(a) = \sum_{i = 1}^d (u^i - a^i) h_i(u), \qquad h_i(a) = \frac{\partial h}{\partial x^i}(a),$$for smooth functions $h_i$. Applying the derivation and using the Leibniz rule shows that its action on $f$ is determined by its action on the coordinate functions. The coefficients are
$$v^i = v[x^i],$$and substitution yields the displayed directional-derivative formula. Thus curve velocities and derivations define canonically isomorphic versions of $T_pM$. This equivalence is treated in detail by Lee (2012, Chapter 3) and Tu (2011, Chapter 3).
The derivation viewpoint immediately implies that tangent vectors annihilate constants:
$$v[c] = 0\qquad\text{for every constant }c.$$7.4 Coordinate transformation law Suppose $x = (x^1, \ldots, x^d)$ and $y = (y^1, \ldots, y^d)$ are two coordinate systems around $p$. The chain rule gives
$$\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right\rvert_p = \sum_{a = 1}^d \frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}(p) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}\right\rvert_p.$$If
$$v = \sum_{i = 1}^d v_x^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} = \sum_{a = 1}^d v_y^a \frac{\partial}{\partial y^a},$$then
$$\boxed{v_y^a = \sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}(p) v_x^i.}$$In matrix notation,
$$[v]_y = D(y \circ x^{-1})_{x(p)} [v]_x.$$The components transform by the Jacobian of the coordinate change. The geometric vector is unchanged.
7.5 Running example: the tangent space of the sphere Let $p \in S^2$ and let $\gamma$ be a curve in $S^2$ with $\gamma(0) = p$. Because $\gamma(t) \cdot \gamma(t) = 1$, differentiation at $t = 0$ gives
$$2p \cdot \dot{\gamma}(0) = 0.$$Every tangent vector $v = \dot{\gamma}(0)$ is therefore orthogonal to $p$. Conversely, if $v \in \mathbb{R}^3$ satisfies $p \cdot v = 0$ and $v \neq 0$, then
$$\gamma(t) = \cos(\lVert v \rVert t) p + \frac{\sin(\lVert v \rVert t)}{\lVert v \rVert} v$$lies on $S^2$, satisfies $\gamma(0) = p$, and has $\dot{\gamma}(0) = v$. For $v = 0$, use the constant curve. Hence
$$\boxed{T_pS^2 = \left\lbrace v \in \mathbb{R}^3 : p \cdot v = 0 \right\rbrace.}$$The intrinsic tangent space is thus naturally identified with the ordinary plane through the origin perpendicular to $p$.
8. Differentials and the tangent bundle Tangent vectors make it possible to differentiate maps between manifolds.
8.1 The differential of a smooth map Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth and let $v = [\gamma] \in T_pM$. Define
$$dF_p(v) = [F \circ \gamma] \in T_{F(p)}N.$$This is well defined: if two curves have the same velocity at $p$, the chain rule shows that their images under $F$ have the same velocity at $F(p)$. The resulting map
$$dF_p : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N$$is linear and is called the differential, pushforward, or tangent map of $F$ at $p$.
Choose coordinates $x = (x^1, \ldots, x^d)$ on $M$ and $y = (y^1, \ldots, y^m)$ on $N$. If
$$F^\alpha = y^\alpha \circ F \circ x^{-1},$$then
$$dF_p\left(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right\rvert_p\right) = \sum_{\alpha = 1}^m \frac{\partial F^\alpha}{\partial x^i}(x(p)) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial y^\alpha}\right\rvert_{F(p)}.$$Thus $dF_p$ is represented by the Jacobian matrix
$$DF(x(p)) = \left(\frac{\partial F^\alpha}{\partial x^i}(x(p))\right)_{\alpha, i}.$$For smooth maps $F : M \to N$ and $G : N \to P$, the chain rule becomes the intrinsic identity
$$\boxed{d(G \circ F)_p = dG_{F(p)} \circ dF_p.}$$When $F$ is a diffeomorphism, $dF_p$ is a linear isomorphism and
$$d(F^{-1})_{F(p)} = (dF_p)^{-1}.$$8.2 The tangent bundle as a manifold The tangent spaces at all points are assembled into the tangent bundle
$$TM = \bigsqcup_{p \in M} T_pM.$$An element of $TM$ is written $(p, v)$ with $v \in T_pM$. The natural projection is
$$\pi : TM \to M, \qquad \pi(p, v) = p.$$A chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ induces a chart on $\pi^{-1}(U) \subseteq TM$:
$$T\varphi : \pi^{-1}(U) \to \varphi(U) \times \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad T\varphi(p, v) = \bigl(\varphi(p), [v]_\varphi\bigr).$$If $y = y(x)$ is a change of coordinates on $M$, the corresponding change of tangent-bundle coordinates is
$$(x, v_x) \longmapsto \bigl(y(x), D y(x) v_x\bigr).$$This map is smooth because $y$ is smooth. These induced charts give $TM$ a natural smooth structure of dimension $2d$:
$$\dim TM = 2d.$$The first $d$ coordinates locate the base point, and the remaining $d$ coordinates record the tangent-vector components. This bundle construction, including its coordinate changes, is standard; see Lee (2012, Chapter 3).
9. Cotangent vectors, differentials, and one-forms A tangent vector is an infinitesimal direction. A cotangent vector is a linear measuring device: it accepts a tangent vector and returns a number.
9.1 Cotangent spaces and the dual basis Definition (cotangent space). The cotangent space at $p$ is the dual vector space
$$\boxed{T_p^*M = \operatorname{Hom}(T_pM, \mathbb{R}).}$$An element $\alpha_p \in T_p^*M$ is a cotangent vector or covector. Its evaluation on $v \in T_pM$ is the canonical pairing
$$\langle \alpha_p, v \rangle = \alpha_p(v).$$This pairing requires no metric. Since $\dim T_pM = d$, we also have $\dim T_p^*M = d$.
The coordinate basis $\left\lbrace \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right\rvert_p \right\rbrace_{i = 1}^d$ determines the dual basis $\left\lbrace (dx^i)p \right\rbrace{i = 1}^d$, characterized by
$$(dx^i)_p\left(\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\right\rvert_p\right) = \delta^i_j.$$Every covector has a unique expansion
$$\boxed{\alpha_p = \sum_{i = 1}^d \alpha_i (dx^i)_p.}$$If $v = \sum_i v^i \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\right\rvert_p$, then
$$\alpha_p(v) = \sum_{i = 1}^d \alpha_i v^i.$$This row-by-column expression is merely the coordinate form of the intrinsic pairing.
9.2 The differential of a function For $f \in C^\infty(M)$, the differential of $f$ at $p$ is the covector $df_p \in T_p^*M$ defined by
$$\boxed{df_p(v) = v[f].}$$If $v = \dot{\gamma}(0)$, then
$$df_p(v) = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_0 f(\gamma(t)).$$Thus $df_p$ records the first-order rate of change of $f$ in every possible tangent direction. In local coordinates,
$$\boxed{df_p = \sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\partial(f \circ \varphi^{-1})}{\partial x^i}\bigl(\varphi(p)\bigr) (dx^i)_p.}$$The notation $dx^i$ is literal: $dx^i$ is the differential of the coordinate function $x^i$. It extracts the corresponding vector component:
$$(dx^i)_p(v) = v[x^i] = v^i.$$For example, on $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $f(x, y) = x^2y + \sin y$. Then
$$df = 2xy\,dx + (x^2 + \cos y)\,dy.$$For $v = a \frac{\partial}{\partial x} + b \frac{\partial}{\partial y}$,
$$df(v) = 2axy + b(x^2 + \cos y).$$The covector $df$ is not itself a direction. It is the rule that measures the change of $f$ in a supplied direction.
9.3 Coordinate transformation law for covectors For two coordinate systems $x = (x^1, \ldots, x^d)$ and $y = (y^1, \ldots, y^d)$, the chain rule gives
$$dy^a = \sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}\,dx^i, \qquad dx^i = \sum_{a = 1}^d \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}\,dy^a.$$If
$$\alpha = \sum_{i = 1}^d \alpha_i^x\,dx^i = \sum_{a = 1}^d \alpha_a^y\,dy^a,$$then
$$\boxed{\alpha_a^y = \sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a} \alpha_i^x.}$$In matrix form,
$$[\alpha]_y = D(x \circ y^{-1})_{y(p)}^T [\alpha]_x.$$Vectors transform by the Jacobian of $y$ with respect to $x$, whereas covector components transform by the transpose of the inverse Jacobian. These laws guarantee
$$\alpha(v) = \sum_i \alpha_i^x v_x^i = \sum_a \alpha_a^y v_y^a.$$The scalar pairing is therefore independent of coordinates.
9.4 The cotangent bundle and one-forms The cotangent spaces form the cotangent bundle
$$T^*M = \bigsqcup_{p \in M} T_p^*M.$$Using coordinates $(x^1, \ldots, x^d)$ on $M$ and covector components $(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_d)$ gives local coordinates
$$(x^1, \ldots, x^d, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_d)$$on $T^*M$. Hence
$$\dim T^*M = 2d.$$Let $\pi_{T^*M} : T^*M \to M$ be the cotangent-bundle projection. A smooth map $\alpha : M \to T^*M$ satisfying $\pi_{T^*M} \circ \alpha = \operatorname{id}_M$ is a smooth one-form. Locally,
$$\alpha = \sum_{i = 1}^d \alpha_i(x)\,dx^i,$$where all coefficient functions $\alpha_i$ are smooth. The one-form $df$ is called exact.
9.5 Pullbacks Let $F : M \to N$ be smooth. The differential moves tangent vectors forward:
$$dF_p : T_pM \to T_{F(p)}N.$$Duality moves covectors in the opposite direction. If $\beta_{F(p)} \in T_{F(p)}^*N$, define
$$(dF_p)^*\beta_{F(p)} \in T_p^*M$$by
$$\bigl((dF_p)^*\beta_{F(p)}\bigr)(v) = \beta_{F(p)}\bigl(dF_p(v)\bigr).$$If $\beta$ is a one-form on $N$, its pullback $F^*\beta$ is the one-form on $M$ given by
$$\boxed{(F^*\beta)_p = (dF_p)^*\beta_{F(p)}.}$$For a smooth function $f : N \to \mathbb{R}$, the chain rule is equivalently
$$d(f \circ F) = F^*(df).$$9.6 Why $df$ is not automatically a gradient In Euclidean calculus, $df$ and $\nabla f$ are often identified because the standard inner product is silently available. On an abstract smooth manifold, they belong to different spaces:
$$df_p \in T_p^*M, \qquad \operatorname{grad}f(p) \in T_pM.$$The smooth structure supplies $df$, but it supplies no canonical isomorphism $T_p^*M \to T_pM$. If a Riemannian metric $g$ is added, the gradient is defined uniquely by
$$g_p(\operatorname{grad}f, v) = df_p(v)\qquad\text{for every }v \in T_pM.$$If $(g^{ij})$ is the inverse of the coordinate matrix $(g_{ij})$, then
$$\operatorname{grad}f = \sum_{i, j = 1}^d g^{ij} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}.$$The distinction between $df$ and $\operatorname{grad}f$ is not cosmetic: it separates what follows from smooth structure alone from what depends on a chosen metric. The dual-space, pullback, and one-form constructions in this section follow Lee (2012, Chapters 3 and 11) and Tu (2011, Chapters 3 and 5).
10. Vector fields and differential equations A single tangent vector gives one infinitesimal direction at one point. A vector field chooses such a direction smoothly at every point and thereby prescribes a differential equation on the manifold.
10.1 Vector fields as sections Definition (smooth vector field). A smooth vector field is a smooth map $X : M \to TM$ satisfying
$$\pi \circ X = \operatorname{id}_M.$$Equivalently, $X(p) = X_p \in T_pM$ for each $p$. In local coordinates,
$$\boxed{X = \sum_{i = 1}^d X^i(x) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}.}$$and $X$ is smooth precisely when its component functions $X^i$ are smooth.
If $y = y(x)$ is another coordinate system, then
$$X_y^a = \sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i} X_x^i.$$The components change, but the section $X$ does not.
10.2 Vector fields as derivations A vector field acts on $f \in C^\infty(M)$ pointwise:
$$X[f](p) = X_p[f].$$In coordinates,
$$X[f] = \sum_{i = 1}^d X^i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^i}.$$It is real-linear and obeys
$$X[fg] = f X[g] + g X[f].$$Conversely, every real-linear derivation $D : C^\infty(M) \to C^\infty(M)$ is induced by a unique smooth vector field. Smooth vector fields can therefore be identified with derivations of the algebra $C^\infty(M)$.
10.3 Integral curves and local existence Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval. A smooth curve $\gamma : I \to M$ is an integral curve of $X$ if
$$\boxed{\dot{\gamma}(t) = X_{\gamma(t)}\qquad\text{for every }t \in I.}$$The initial-value problem through $p \in M$ is
$$\dot{\gamma}(t) = X_{\gamma(t)}, \qquad \gamma(0) = p.$$In local coordinates $\gamma(t) = (x^1(t), \ldots, x^d(t))$, this becomes
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}x^i}{\mathrm{d}t} = X^i(x^1(t), \ldots, x^d(t)), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, d.$$Because the component functions are smooth, they are locally Lipschitz. The Euclidean existence-and-uniqueness theorem therefore yields a unique local solution through each initial point. Solutions obtained in different charts agree on overlaps by uniqueness, so they combine into an intrinsic integral curve on $M$.
Each initial point $p$ has a unique maximal integral curve
$$\gamma_p : I_p \to M,$$where $I_p \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is the largest open interval containing $0$ on which the solution exists.
10.4 Complete fields and flows A vector field is complete if $I_p = \mathbb{R}$ for every $p \in M$. Smoothness alone does not imply completeness. On $\mathbb{R}$,
$$X = x^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial x}$$has the solution
$$x(t) = \frac{x_0}{1 - x_0 t},$$which blows up at $t = 1/x_0$ when $x_0 > 0$. By contrast, every smooth vector field on a compact manifold without boundary is complete.
The set $\mathcal{D} = \left\lbrace (t, p) \in \mathbb{R} \times M : t \in I_p \right\rbrace$ is open in $\mathbb{R} \times M$. On this domain, set
$$\Phi(t, p) = \gamma_p(t).$$The map $\Phi$ is the local flow generated by $X$. It satisfies
$$\Phi(0, p) = p, \qquad \Phi(t, \Phi(s, p)) = \Phi(t + s, p)$$whenever both sides are defined. The field is recovered from its flow by
$$X_p = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right\rvert_{t = 0}\Phi(t, p).$$If $X$ is complete, $\Phi$ is defined on all of $\mathbb{R} \times M$. Each time-$t$ map $\Phi_t(p) = \Phi(t, p)$ is a diffeomorphism and
$$\Phi_t^{-1} = \Phi_{-t}.$$Thus a complete vector field generates a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms. The local existence theorem, smooth dependence, maximal flow domain, and compact-manifold completeness result are proved in Lee (2012, Chapter 9).
10.5 Equilibria and conserved functions A point $p$ is an equilibrium if $X_p = 0$. The integral curve through an equilibrium is constant.
Along any integral curve,
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} f(\gamma(t)) = X[f](\gamma(t)).$$Therefore a smooth function $f$ is constant along every integral curve exactly when
$$\boxed{X[f] = 0.}$$This condition is intrinsic and requires no coordinates or metric.
10.6 The Lie bracket For smooth vector fields $X$ and $Y$, define
$$\boxed{[X, Y][f] = X[Y[f]] - Y[X[f]].}$$Although each composition on the right is generally a second-order operator, their second-order terms cancel. The result is a derivation and hence another vector field. In local coordinates,
$$[X, Y] = \sum_{i = 1}^d \left(\sum_{j = 1}^d X^j \frac{\partial Y^i}{\partial x^j} - \sum_{j = 1}^d Y^j \frac{\partial X^i}{\partial x^j}\right) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}.$$The Lie bracket is antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity:
$$[X, Y] = -[Y, X], \qquad [X, [Y, Z]] + [Y, [Z, X]] + [Z, [X, Y]] = 0.$$It is not $C^\infty(M)$-bilinear. Instead,
$$[X, fY] = f[X, Y] + X[f] Y.$$Geometrically, $[X, Y]$ measures the infinitesimal failure of the flows of $X$ and $Y$ to commute. The local flows commute wherever both compositions are defined if and only if $[X, Y] = 0$; see Lee (2012, Chapters 8 and 9).
10.7 Running example: rotation on the sphere On $S^2$, consider
$$X(x, y, z) = (-y, x, 0).$$The field is tangent to the sphere because
$$(x, y, z) \cdot (-y, x, 0) = 0.$$Its integral-curve equations are
$$\dot{x} = -y, \qquad \dot{y} = x, \qquad \dot{z} = 0.$$Through $(x_0, y_0, z_0) \in S^2$, the solution is
$$x(t) = x_0 \cos t - y_0 \sin t, \qquad y(t) = x_0 \sin t + y_0 \cos t, \qquad z(t) = z_0.$$The flow rotates the sphere around the $z$-axis. The height function $f(x, y, z) = z$ is conserved because $X[f] = 0$. In this one example, the abstract notions of tangent vector, vector field, integral curve, flow, and first integral become a single familiar motion.
11. Submanifolds and manifolds with boundary Not every subset of a manifold is itself a manifold. The subset must sit locally like a linear coordinate slice.
11.1 Embedded submanifolds Let $M$ be a smooth $d$-manifold and let $S \subseteq M$. We call $S$ an embedded submanifold of dimension $k$ if, for every $p \in S$, there is a chart $(U, \varphi)$ on $M$ such that
$$\varphi(U \cap S) = \varphi(U) \cap \bigl(\mathbb{R}^k \times \left\lbrace 0 \right\rbrace^{d - k}\bigr).$$Such a chart is called a slice chart or adapted chart. In these coordinates, $S$ is locally obtained by setting $d - k$ coordinates equal to zero.
The tangent space of $S$ is naturally a linear subspace of the ambient tangent space:
$$T_pS \subseteq T_pM.$$11.2 Regular level sets The regular-level-set theorem gives a powerful way to construct submanifolds. Let $F : M^d \to N^m$ be smooth, and let $q \in N$. If
$$dF_p : T_pM \to T_qN$$is surjective for every $p \in F^{-1}(q)$, then $q$ is a regular value, and $F^{-1}(q)$ is an embedded submanifold of dimension $d - m$. Moreover,
$$T_pF^{-1}(q) = \ker dF_p.$$For the sphere, define $F : \mathbb{R}^{d + 1} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $F(x) = \lVert x \rVert^2$. Then $S^d = F^{-1}(1)$ and
$$dF_p(v) = 2p \cdot v.$$For $p \in S^d$, this linear map is nonzero and hence surjective onto $\mathbb{R}$. Therefore $S^d$ is a smooth submanifold of dimension $d$, and
$$T_pS^d = \ker dF_p = \left\lbrace v \in \mathbb{R}^{d + 1} : p \cdot v = 0 \right\rbrace.$$This recovers the tangent-space calculation from Section 7 in a more general framework. The result used here is also called the regular level set theorem or regular value theorem; see Lee (2012, Chapter 5).
11.3 Manifolds with boundary For $d \geq 1$, a manifold with boundary is locally modeled on relatively open subsets of the closed half-space
$$\mathbb{H}^d = \left\lbrace (x^1, \ldots, x^d) \in \mathbb{R}^d : x^d \geq 0 \right\rbrace.$$A boundary chart is a homeomorphism $\varphi : U \to \varphi(U) \subseteq \mathbb{H}^d$, where $\varphi(U)$ is open in the subspace topology of $\mathbb{H}^d$. Smoothness of transition maps is defined by requiring local smooth extensions to open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$. A point corresponding to $x^d > 0$ is an interior point; a point corresponding to $x^d = 0$ is a boundary point. This classification is independent of the chosen boundary chart. The set of boundary points, denoted by $\partial M$, is a smooth $(d - 1)$-manifold without boundary.
For example, the closed interval $[0, 1]$ is a one-dimensional manifold with boundary
$$\partial[0, 1] = \left\lbrace 0, 1 \right\rbrace.$$The closed ball
$$\overline{B}^d = \left\lbrace x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \lVert x \rVert \leq 1 \right\rbrace$$is a $d$-manifold with boundary $\partial \overline{B}^d = S^{d - 1}$. It is not a manifold without boundary, because a neighborhood of a boundary point is not homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$. For the precise extension-based definition and the invariance of boundary, see Lee (2012, Chapter 1).
12. What smooth structure provides—and what it does not A smooth manifold is already rich enough to support:
smooth real-valued functions and smooth maps; smooth curves and their velocities; tangent and cotangent bundles; differentials and pullbacks; vector fields, one-forms, and higher differential forms; Lie brackets of vector fields; ordinary differential equations and local flows. All of these constructions are canonical consequences of the smooth structure: a smooth map automatically has a differential, a smooth function automatically has a one-form $df$, and two vector fields automatically have a Lie bracket. No metric or ambient Euclidean space is needed.
Other familiar notions require additional choices:
Desired notion Additional structure usually required Lengths, angles, distances, and gradients A Riemannian metric Spacetime intervals and causal cones A Lorentzian metric Parallel transport and covariant differentiation A connection Integration of top-degree forms An orientation; alternatively, a density for orientation-free integration Complex-analytic coordinates A complex structure Hamiltonian vector fields and symplectic area A symplectic form These extra structures are not generally unique. The same smooth manifold can carry many Riemannian metrics, connections, symplectic forms, or complex structures—and sometimes it can carry none of a requested kind. Choosing one therefore adds geometric information that cannot be recovered from the smooth atlas alone.
In particular, a bare smooth manifold has no canonical distance, no canonical notion of orthogonality, and no canonical gradient vector. It tells us what it means to differentiate, but not how to measure. This is why $df$ appeared before the gradient: $df$ belongs to smooth calculus itself, whereas $\operatorname{grad}f$ belongs to Riemannian geometry.
The hierarchy is
$$\text{set} \longrightarrow \text{topological space} \longrightarrow \text{topological manifold} \longrightarrow \text{smooth manifold} \longrightarrow \text{manifold with additional geometry}.$$Each arrow represents additional data or additional axioms. Passing to the right preserves the earlier notions while making new questions meaningful. For example, topology lets us ask whether a sequence converges; smooth structure lets us differentiate; a metric lets us measure lengths and angles.
13. Common misconceptions “A manifold must be a surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$.” No. A manifold is defined intrinsically by its topology and compatible charts. A surface embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is an important example, not the general definition.
“A chart is one coordinate.” Not exactly. A chart $(U, \varphi)$ supplies an entire local coordinate system. Its component functions $x^1, \ldots, x^d$ are the individual coordinates.
“The dimension of a manifold is its ambient dimension.” No. Dimension counts independent local coordinates. The sphere $S^2 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ has intrinsic dimension two.
“Every subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is automatically a manifold.” No. Singularities, crossings, corners, and changes of local dimension can violate the local Euclidean condition. Some subsets are manifolds with boundary or corners; others are not manifolds at all.
“A smooth manifold must have one global coordinate system.” No. Most interesting manifolds require multiple charts. Smooth geometry is designed precisely to combine local coordinate calculations into global statements.
“A tangent vector is an arrow joining two points of the manifold.” No. A tangent vector is based at one point and represents an infinitesimal velocity there. In general, two points of a manifold cannot be subtracted to produce a tangent vector.
“The differential $df$ and the gradient $\operatorname{grad}f$ are the same.” Not without a metric. The differential is a covector supplied by the smooth structure; the gradient is a vector obtained from that covector after choosing a Riemannian metric.
14. Final perspective A smooth manifold is not “a curved Euclidean space” in the sense of requiring a surrounding space or a metric. It is a space whose local pieces can be described by Euclidean coordinates and whose coordinate descriptions agree through smooth transition maps.
The logical architecture is now visible:
topology provides neighborhoods and continuity; charts provide local Euclidean descriptions; transition maps make the coordinate descriptions compatible; the resulting smooth structure defines smooth functions and maps; curves and derivations produce tangent vectors; duality produces cotangent vectors and differentials; smooth sections produce vector fields and differential equations. Coordinates are indispensable computational tools, but an intrinsic object or property must transform consistently when the chart changes. The true object is the manifold; coordinates are temporary languages used to describe it.
The central message can therefore be sharpened to
$$\boxed{\text{A smooth manifold is a globally defined space on which local Euclidean calculus is coordinate independent.}}$$That local-to-global principle is the foundation on which the rest of differential geometry is built.
References Lee, J. M. (2011). Introduction to Topological Manifolds (2nd ed.). Graduate Texts in Mathematics. Springer. DOI. Lee, J. M. (2012). Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2nd ed.). Graduate Texts in Mathematics. Springer. DOI. Tu, L. W. (2011). An Introduction to Manifolds (2nd ed.). Universitext. Springer. DOI.
summary: Abstract. A smooth manifold is a space that may be globally curved or topologically complicated while remaining locally indistinguishable from Euclidean space. This post introduces this concept from first principles. We begin with topology, charts, transition maps, and atlases; then define smooth functions and smooth maps without assuming that the manifold sits inside a larger Euclidean space. From there, we construct tangent and cotangent spaces, differentials, vector fields, integral curves, flows, and Lie brackets. The sphere serves as a recurring example, allowing each abstract definition to be compared with familiar geometry. The central theme is that coordinates make calculations possible, while compatibility under coordinate changes makes the resulting mathematics intrinsic.
